How logging & calibration work

Two kinds of log (the Type column):
💧 Water report — where the water is right now, or the receding line. Shows on the map; does not change the forecast.
🎯 High-water line — the peak mud/debris line after a flood. This is what can calibrate the model.

Manage actions on each row:
⚓ Make crest anchor — promotes a high-water log into a crest anchor (the green section). This is the only thing that re-fits the forecast. It prefills the green form; you confirm the flood peak crest and press ＋ Add crest anchor.
✎ Edit — review/fix every field, including GPS.
🔖 Track location — saves that spot as a named, tracked location (appears in the Section-3 pick-lists). Nothing to do with showing GPS.
🗑 Delete — removes the log (asks to confirm).

The green crest-anchors section holds the confirmed marks that calibrate the model. When you (admin) add one it applies immediately and appears there with a ✕ to remove it. Marks added by others wait for your approval on the moderation page. ↺ Clear all anchors wipes them and returns to the 2013 seed calibration.

Map colors: 🔵 water report · 🟠 high-water log · 🔴 ◆ crest anchor.

From the phone logger: choosing 🎯 High-water mark sends it here as a High-water log (Type), ready to promote to a crest anchor.

1 · The gauge chain — your early-warning ladder

Each gauge upstream buys lead time: the flood wave reaches Uvalde/Asherton first, then Cotulla, then the Miles Ranch reach — arriving ~2 days before Tilden crests downstream. Watching the upstream gauges gives you several days’ warning on a rising flood.

namegroundnow (observed, else est.)at crest (forecast)
“now” priority (best first): ① 💧 blue observed = someone logged water there, with how long ago — ground truth. ② “NWM est.” = modeled at the ranch's own reach (lag-free). ③ plain “est.” = only the Tilden gauge, which sits ~a day downstream, so on a rising river an “est. dry” spot may already be wet. Trust eyes first — and log it so it turns blue.
Geometry: each spot's river-mile is measured along the authentic USGS Nueces channel trace (NHD, HUC 1211 — reach sinuosity 1.91), and its sideways distance out to a slue/floodplain (shown as “off-channel”) is projected onto the channel rather than inflating its depth.

6 · Advanced · model calibration

Everyday water & crest logging now lives in 📍 Your places & marks up above. This section is the advanced calibration engine — it fine-tunes the forecast from crest anchors (for admins).

⚙ Show advanced calibration tools
🎯 High-water mark — makes the forecast smarter (optional) You don't have to do this — the forecast already works. But after a flood, a high-water mark makes every future forecast sharper. You can't miss the window: the mud/debris line stays on posts, fences and trees for weeks, so you record it whenever it's safe to walk out — no need to be there at the crest.
▸ How to add one (3 steps)
1. After the water drops, go to a spot you can point to on the map (a gate, a pen, a pole, the pad).
2. Find the mud/debris line — the highest the water reached. Measure how far above the ground that line sits (0 if it's right at ground level).
3. Below: pick that spot, enter that height, and this flood's peak Tilden crest (tap “⤓ peak” to fill it), then Add.
That's it. You're telling the model “at this exact place, the flood's high-water line was here, and the gauge crested at that number.” It doesn't matter that the ranch and the gauge peak at different times — a mark plus that flood's crest is all it needs.
Uses every “Report water now” pin at once: for each spot it takes the highest water reported there (random samples converge on the true high-water line) and pairs it with this flood’s peak crest. Do it near/after the crest. In shared mode the built marks wait for your approval on the admin page.

⚙ Customize the “at the ranch” landmark tiers (tap)
Engine. Water elevation at a point = Tilden stage + 183.10 + (slope × river-miles that point sits above the gauge). Depth = that − ground (USGS 3DEP LiDAR). “Slope” starts at 1.36 ft per river-mile (fit to the 2013 ranch marks) and re-fits by weighted least-squares every time you log a sighting. “Water rise above gauge” (offset) = ground + observed depth − 183.10 − gauge reading — the one number the model learns. Mechanism buttons set the crest band from historic analogs (2026 dry-routed, 2018 wet-routed, 2002/2013 local-rain, 1967 Beulah tropical). Custom coordinates carry ±3 ft until a nearby sighting tightens them. Decision aid only — defer to official NWS/NOAA warnings for life-safety.

📖 The flood models — what each one does

Every model drapes a water surface over the 1 m LiDAR terrain and shows where the ground sits below it. They differ only in the reach water-surface slope they use (how much higher the flood stands per river-mile upstream of Tilden).

🟦 Calibrated (your marks) — the default, best estimate. Starts from the LiDAR terrain and re-fits the slope from your crest anchors: surveyed marks weighted most, off-channel and outlier marks down-weighted. It improves every time you add a verified high-water mark. This is what the main blue fill uses unless you switch it.

🟧 Raw LiDAR — the starting point, no crowd calibration. Same LiDAR terrain, but with the model’s default slope (~2.09 ft per river-mile, derived from the authentic USGS/NHD channel geometry and the 2013 surveyed line). Use it to see the flood before any of your marks nudged it.

“Raw LiDAR” (in Flood-fill model) and “LiDAR” (in Advanced compare) are the SAME model — one sets the main blue fill; the other overlays it as a coloured comparison layer so you can see it against the others.

🟪 Baseline (seed) — the 2013-only seed calibration, before any crowd marks. Overlay it to see how far your marks have moved the forecast.

📊 Model vs marks — a residual check: a dot at each of your marks, coloured by how far the model’s predicted depth is from what you actually logged (green ≤ 0.5 ft · amber ≤ 1.5 · red > 1.5). Shows where the model agrees and where it doesn’t.

🛰 NOAA FIM — NOAA’s official Flood Inundation Map footprint for this reach, when published. An independent, authoritative cross-check against the model.

🌊 Shade by depth — not a different model; it recolours whichever fill is on so lighter blue = shallow, darker blue = deeper water at the current crest.

Rule of thumb: use Calibrated for the working forecast; use Raw LiDAR / Baseline to understand how your marks are shaping it; use Model vs marks and FIM to sanity-check it.

📖 Terms & definitions

Tilden gauge (TILT2) — the USGS river gauge downstream of the ranch. Its stage is the water height it reads, in feet. Everything keys off it.

Flood stage — the stage at which the river starts to flood at Tilden: 14 ft. Below that = in-bank.

Crest — the peak stage of a flood (the highest the gauge reaches before it falls).

rm (river-mile) — distance measured along the river channel upstream of the Tilden gauge. The ranch is ~11.7 rm up.

off-channel — how far a spot sits sideways from the main channel (out toward a slue/floodplain).

rise — for a crest mark: how much higher the flood's water surface stood at that spot than the Tilden reading, because the spot is upstream. rise ÷ rm ≈ the reach's water-surface slope (~2 ft/mile here).

NOW (hub column) — what's happening at a place right now: a logged water depth, or an estimate from the live gauge.

AT CREST (hub column) — the forecast depth at that place if Tilden crests at the chosen level. Set the level with the crest box above the table.

Depth pills — dry the ground is still above the water (freeboard) · under flooded, water over the ground · amber within ½ ft of flooding · deep a logged water depth.

Water sighting — a report of where the water is right now. Shows on the map; does not change the forecast on its own.

High-water line — the debris/mud line marking the peak a flood reached at a spot (recorded after it recedes).

Crest anchor — a high-water line paired with that flood's peak Tilden crest, used to calibrate (tune) the forecast slope. The only thing that re-fits the model.

Watch spot — a saved place (name + elevation) you want to keep an eye on, with no reading logged yet.

NWM — the NOAA National Water Model; an independent modeled flow for the ranch's own river reach.

Fused forecast — one combined outlook blending the Tilden gauge/forecast, the NWM reach flow, and your calibration marks.

FIM — NOAA's Flood Inundation Mapping (satellite/model footprint), shown when available.

Flood-fill model — the blue inundation on the map. Calibrated follows your marks; Raw LiDAR uses the bare terrain model.

Flood front / wave — the leading edge of flood-stage water travelling down the channel (Cotulla → ranch → Tilden). It's why the ranch floods before Tilden crests.

Not sure about a term not listed here? Tell George and we'll add it.

How to use this model

What this is. The Miles Ranch sits in the ungauged 100-mile reach between the Cotulla and Tilden river gauges, so NOAA forecasts at those gauges but not on your land. This tool bridges that gap: it reads the live gauges and translates them into a predicted water depth and timing at any point on the ranch, calibrated on the confirmed 2013 high-water marks. It is a decision aid — official NWS/NOAA warnings always govern life-safety.

1 · The gauge chain

The row of gauges from the Hill Country down to Three Rivers. Each one upstream is earlier warning — Asherton crests ~8 days before the ranch, Cotulla ~5. The gauges show stage in feet (height on that gauge). The Ranch box has no gauge, so it shows its current modeled status from the live Tilden reading (DRY / RISING / HIGH / FLOODING / FLOODED) — this is “now,” not a forecast. The forecast for a predicted crest lives in Section 3. Gauges auto-update every 15 minutes; the links open the official NOAA pages.

2 · Which kind of flood (mechanism)

The same amount of water behaves very differently depending on how the flood is made. Auto reads the mechanism from the live gauges (mainly the Tilden-vs-Cotulla flow ratio) and picks it for you, explaining why. Tap any button to override for a “what-if” — e.g. force “gaining reach” or “tropical” to stress-test. A green banner means auto; amber means you’ve overridden, with a link back to auto. The two amplifying regimes — a gaining reach (extra water enters between Cotulla and Tilden, from local rain or a tributary like the Frio) and tropical — are the dangerous ones: the ranch can flood even when the upstream gauge looks modest. The names describe the river’s behaviour, not necessarily rain falling on the ranch itself.

3 · Forecast & your locations

Slide the Cotulla crest and the mechanism converts it to a predicted Tilden crest (the big red number) — or drag the Tilden slider directly for free what-ifs. Below, the big number is the predicted water-surface elevation at the ranch. The ladder lists every location high-to-low; the blue line is the water surface, rows above it stay dry (green), rows below flood (red) with the depth. Save scenario stores a crest+mechanism you can reload later. ＋ Add location lets you add any spot by coordinates with an auto-fetched ground elevation.

4 · Satellite map

Your locations on aerial imagery, colored green (dry) or red (flooded) for the current scenario. Tap the map anywhere to drop a new location — it grabs the coordinates and fetches the elevation for you.

5 · Reach profile

A side-view of the water surface down the whole chain. Pills between gauges are travel time; ⚠ marks a gauge above flood stage; kcfs is live flow. 🌊 is the flood-stage front — how far downstream water has reached flood stage. It slides continuously between gauges (so it can sit on the ranch), and reads ▶ advancing or ◀ receding from the last 18 h of gauge trend. Note it marks the flood-stage boundary, not the very first ripple of the rise, which runs a bit ahead of it.

6 · Report water & teach the model

Two separate things. A live report (“water is here now”) drops a blue pin on the shared map so everyone can see where the water is — it does not change the forecast. A high-water mark is how the model actually learns: after a flood peaks, you mark the high-water line at a known spot and give that flood's peak Tilden crest, and the tool re-fits its water-surface slope. The reason it must be peak-to-peak is that the ranch floods about a day ahead of the gauge, so a live reading compared to the live gauge would over-steepen the model. In shared mode, high-water marks go to an admin for approval before they move the forecast; live reports appear on the map right away.

7 · Historical context

Every Tilden flood on record since 1935, ranked against your scenario, with a plain-English read of where it sits. ★ marks the five benchmark floods with full detail. Tap any event for its story and a compare/contrast to what you’re watching. After a flood ends and NOAA logs the official crest, press “Update record from NOAA” to pull it in.

Does it refresh itself?

Yes. The gauges auto-pull when you open it and re-pull every 15 minutes while the tab is open, and the forecast, ladder, map and mechanism all recompute in place — no page reload needed. In shared (Firebase) mode, approved sightings appear live for everyone. Your locations, sightings and saved scenarios are stored on your device and persist across reloads (they are not auto-cleared). Use the button below to wipe them.

A note on accuracy

Saved ranch features carry about ±1.2 ft (calibrated on 2013); a brand-new custom coordinate carries about ±3 ft until a nearby sighting tightens it. The forecast assumes no fresh rain falls in the reach — if that changes, switch the mechanism to “local rain” and watch for sightings to confirm.
